concept.name: Deep out-of-the-money option
concept.definition: A deep out-of-the-money option is an option whose strike is far from the current underlying price, so it has no intrinsic value, a very small delta, and a premium close to zero that consists only of time value. 'Deep' is informal; no fixed threshold defines it.
concept.intuition: A deep OTM option is a cheap tail-risk ticket: it almost always expires worthless but can multiply in value during extreme moves.
concept.mechanics: Price is dominated by the implied probability of a large move (fat tails and skew make these options systematically pricier than lognormal models suggest). Delta-based margin systems treat, e.g., ten deep OTM options with delta 0.20 as two futures-equivalent contracts.
concept.failure_modes: Black-Scholes-style models underprice deep OTM options when return distributions have fat tails — a key lesson of the 1987 crash. Deep OTM quotes are wide and stale, so mark-to-model and end-of-day pricing can be unreliable.
concept.misconceptions: A near-zero price does not mean 'free optionality': the tiny premium reflects a tiny probability-weighted payoff, and repeatedly selling deep OTM options concentrates exposure to rare, severe losses (picking up pennies in front of a steamroller).
concept.example: With the S&P 500 at 5,000, a 30-day 4,000-strike put is deep OTM and may trade for a few cents, yet it is exactly the instrument that pays off in a crash.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
